accroche: In 1710, London creates the first copyright. The booksellers had asked for it to save their monopoly; they come out stripped of it.
contenu_vulgarise:
London, in the years after 1695. Parliament has just let the Licensing Act of 1662 expire, and with it the regime that organized all of English printing. For more than thirty years, a guild, the Stationers' Company, had run the trade: a book entered in its register belonged to the bookseller who had put it there, with no time limit, and nothing could legally be printed outside it. The expiry in 1695 brought down censorship and the monopoly together. The London booksellers, suddenly exposed to wildcat reprinting, spent the next fifteen years asking Parliament to restore their perpetual right.

## What Parliament grants them, and what it takes away

The statute passed on April 5, 1710, and in force from April 10, is titled “An Act for the Encouragement of Learning, by Vesting the Copies of Printed Books in the Authors or Purchasers of such Copies, during the Times therein mentioned.” The title already holds both reversals. First the words “in the Authors”: the right is attached to the author, no longer to the bookseller who entered the book in the register. Then “during the Times therein mentioned”: it is limited in time.

The limits are precise. A new book carries fourteen years of exclusive right, renewable for another fourteen if the author is still alive at the end of the first term. Books already in print when the Act passed receive twenty-one years, and nothing beyond. Once these terms run out, the work falls into the public domain, a notion this text brings into being by implication, simply by setting an end.

The booksellers had asked for perpetuity and got a clock. They had asked for a guild right and got an author's right, which they now had to buy from someone before they could exploit it.

## A text of cultural policy, not of protection

The word “Encouragement” in the title states the goal Parliament had set itself: to promote the production and spread of knowledge. The preamble explicitly aims at encouraging learned men to compose and write useful books. Literary property is not laid down as a natural right waiting to be recognized. It is a tool, a temporary monopoly granted because it produces books, and withdrawn as soon as it stops being necessary.

This is the exact opposite of today's common intuition, which sees copyright as a protection granted to the creator and its length as an act of generosity. The first copyright in history was born as a limit imposed on those who already held power over books. Its term was not the measure of what was being given to the author. It was the measure of what was being taken back from the publishers.

Two and a half centuries of successive extensions have turned the relationship around, to the point that the question asked in 1710, how long does a monopoly remain useful, is hardly asked in those terms anymore.

carte.punch: The first copyright was a limit imposed on publishers, not a gift to authors.
carte.idee: The booksellers of London asked Parliament to restore their perpetual monopoly over books. The Statute of Anne, in force on April 10, 1710, gives them the opposite: a right attached to the author, and limited to fourteen years, renewable once.

quiz.question: What did the London booksellers ask Parliament for in the years leading up to the Statute of Anne?
choix: The restoration of their perpetual right over the books they had entered in their guild's register
The creation of a new right for authors, whose exploitation they hoped to buy
A fixed term of fourteen years, judged enough to recoup the cost of a print run
The abolition of royal censorship, which delayed the publication of their books
quiz.explication: After the Licensing Act expired in 1695, the Stationers' Company had lost its monopoly and asked Parliament to restore it with no time limit. The 1710 text gave it the opposite of what it asked for: a right attached to the author, and limited in time.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What terms does the Statute of Anne grant to books already in print when it was passed, and to new books?
choix: Twenty-one years for books already in print, fourteen years renewable once for new books
Fourteen years for books already in print, twenty-one non-renewable years for new books
Ten years for all books, with no distinction between old and new
Perpetuity for books already in print, seven years for new books
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text sets two regimes: twenty-one years for books already in print when it passed, and fourteen years renewable once, if the author is still alive, for new books.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what does the word Encouragement in the official title of the Statute of Anne mean?
choix: That it is a financial reward paid directly by the Crown to authors
That Parliament's aim is to promote the production and spread of knowledge
That it encourages booksellers to invest in new printing presses
That it is a piece of propaganda meant to reassure authors after 1695
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The word Encouragement states the goal Parliament had set itself, to promote the production and spread of knowledge, the preamble explicitly aiming at encouraging learned men to compose useful books.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the entry characterize the nature of the copyright created in 1710, in contrast with today's intuition?
choix: As a natural right of the author, which Parliament merely recognizes officially
As an honorary reward, with no real economic consequence for the author
As a religious privilege, inherited from the practices of ecclesiastical censorship
As a temporary monopoly, a tool of cultural policy and not a protection owed to the creator
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry insists: literary property is not laid down as a natural right but as a tool, a temporary monopoly granted because it produces books and withdrawn as soon as it stops being necessary, the opposite of today's intuition.
